subject: Ingress transport decision: operational playbook for Polaris pilot
messages:
From: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>
To: Mira Gonzales <mira@polarishealth.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 16 May 2026 09:14:00 -0700
Subject: Ingress transport options for Polaris pilot

Hi Mira —

Thanks again for the time yesterday. Per our conversation, I put together a short operational summary of the three transport options we're seeing most commonly for Private deployments (VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink / interface endpoints, and site-to-site VPN). Attached is a compact matrix (polaris_ingress_matrix.csv) and a suggested checklist for the pilot network team (network-topology-diagram.pdf referenced).

Top-level tradeoffs (very condensed):
- VPC peering: lowest operational complexity for intra-region hosts; straight-forward routing, slightly larger blast radius if not segmented; requires peering policies and CIDR planning.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): best per-API isolation and narrow exposure surface; adds management of endpoint services and ENIs, good for cross-account access without route table exposure.
- Site-to-site VPN: lower integration effort for on-prem MPLS or legacy gear; higher variability in latency, throughput caps, and dependent on customer edge hardware.

For Polaris pilot we recommended prioritizing: 1) predictable latency & observability, 2) simplest automated rollbacks, 3) limiting scope of access (least privilege). Based on that, our internal leaning is: PrivateLink for initial pilot API surfaces (inbound inference egress to customer), paired with a controlled peering path for backend control plane if Polaris wants native VPC-to-VPC traffic. VPN can be a fallback if there are policy or hardware constraints.

Questions for you so we can finalize a recommendation:
- Do you have a preferred CIDR plan or will Polaris accept our suggested /24s for the pilot VPC?
- Is there a team that manages the MPLS/CPE we should loop into the call?
- Any strict constraint on egress IP continuity for your firewall rules?

I'll pull in an operational playbook draft for your network team (short doc: redwood-playbook-ingress.md) once you confirm the preferred path. If helpful, happy to schedule a 30m runbook walkthrough with your NetOps next week.

Thanks,

Ben —

Appreciate the rapid summary. A few clarifications from our side:
- Polaris prefers keeping control-plane traffic inside our VPCs where possible; we have strict monitoring on endpoint ENIs but can accept PrivateLink for service endpoints if the source IPs are predictable.
- Our on-prem MPLS terminates in two DCs (east + central). We will need consistent egress IPs when we add firewall rules for the pilot; does PrivateLink provide a stable egress address we can rely on?
- For latency: inference calls are sensitive (P50 ~30-40ms target). We want to avoid hops that add jitter.

NetOps (cc) — please weigh in on whether your CPE can handle IPsec tunnels at sustained 1 Gbps; if so, VPN remains an option.

From: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.com>

Date: Mon, 18 May 2026 13:35:00 -07:00
Subject: RE: Ingress transport options for Polaris pilot (internal)

Ben — good thread. Quick internal notes before we respond:

1) Egress stability for PrivateLink: PrivateLink itself exposes an ENI in the customer's account; egress IP continuity depends on where the traffic originates. If Polaris requires a single static egress IP block for firewall allowlisting, the usual pattern is to pair PrivateLink with a NATing path behind the endpoint or use a small controlled peering/VPC egress VPC that provides stable NAT IPs. That adds one extra hop but preserves the least-exposure principle.

2) Latency/Jitter: VPN introduces more variance (CPU on CPE, MTU mismatches, rekey pauses). For P50 targets ~30ms, peering or PrivateLink are significantly more consistent. Peering wins if both sides are in same region and route tables are well-managed.

3) Ops & rollback: PrivateLink enables granular rollback by removing service permissions or deleting endpoint connections; peering requires route removals which can be faster but has broader routing implications. For pilot we can recommend PrivateLink + egress-VPC NAT for stable egress IPs.

Action: Ben, draft the response proposing PrivateLink + small egress VPC (we own the NAT addresses, helps allowlists) as the default, with VPN as contingency and peering as an option if Polaris wants low-latency intra-VPC traffic without additional NAT. Attach the playbook and a quick decision checklist.

— Lauren
VP, Customer Solutions | Redwood Inference

Mira / NetOps —

Thanks for the quick responses. Summary and recommended next steps below (short version):

Recommendation: PrivateLink for the pilot API surface, paired with a small Redwood-managed egress VPC that provides a stable NAT pool for your firewall allowlist. Rationale: preserves minimal exposure, gives you predictable egress IPs, and keeps latency consistent for inference calls.

Fallbacks/alternatives:
- VPC peering: good for low-latency backend interconnect if you want native IP addressing between VPCs; consider if you plan heavy inter-VPC traffic beyond API calls.
- Site-to-site IPsec VPN: acceptable when customer policy or hardware prevents PrivateLink; expect higher jitter and require a CPE capable of sustained throughput and monitoring of IPsec health.

Attachments included for your team: redwood-playbook-ingress.md (runbook & rollback steps), network-topology-diagram.pdf (illustrative pilot topology), polaris_ingress_matrix.csv (detailed comparison + checklist).

Proposed next step: 30-minute technical runbook with your NetOps to confirm CIDRs and NAT egress IPs. I blocked two slots on our side: Wed 20 May 10:00-10:30 PT and Thu 21 May 14:00-14:30 PT — please tell us which works or propose a time.

If NetOps confirms CPE can do sustained 1 Gbps tunnels and you'd rather avoid constructing an egress VPC, we can present a VPN design as Plan B.

Cheers,
